slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Used in routine screening of liver health and to help diagnose or monitor liver problems, usually as part of a liver function panel. Some liver diseases raise ALT before symptoms appear, so the test may help detect them early.

Ordered when there are symptoms of liver damage (for example jaundice, dark urine or light-colored stool, abdominal swelling or pain, frequent itching) or a high risk of liver damage: family history of liver disease, alcohol use disorder, obesity, diabetes, medicines that can harm the liver, or hepatitis or exposure to it.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: ALT is usually measured together with AST in a liver function panel. Because ALT is found mostly in the liver, it checks more specifically for liver damage.
Physiology: ALT (alanine transaminase) is an enzyme found mainly in the liver, and its blood level is usually low. When liver cells are damaged, they release ALT into the bloodstream.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: High: Possible causes of liver damage with a high ALT: hepatitis, infection, cirrhosis, liver cancer, other liver diseases, a lack of blood flow to the liver, certain medicines (such as cholesterol or pain medicines) and poisons.

High: Cytolytic (hepatocellular) pattern: ALT and AST are raised disproportionately to alkaline phosphatase. It points to liver-cell injury; the work-up looks for viral hepatitis, fatty liver disease, alcohol, medicines and other causes.
Low: Low ALT is not common and may lead to further testing. Possible causes include vitamin B6 deficiency and chronic kidney disease.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines taken; some may need to be paused, but only on the provider's advice. Because ALT is usually ordered with other blood tests, fasting for several hours is often required.

Interferences: A high ALT does not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Age, sex, weight, certain medicines and dietary supplements, intense exercise and the phase of the menstrual cycle can affect the result.
Limitations: ALT is interpreted together with the other liver tests. It may help tell acute from chronic liver problems, but the ALT level does not reflect how much of the liver is damaged.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: When liver test results are abnormal, the provider compares all the measured substances to look for patterns that suggest different types of liver conditions. Liver function tests alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

The liver’s synthetic function (hepatocellular failure pattern) is judged not by enzymes but by proteins the liver makes: albumin and prothrombin time (PT/INR); bilirubin also reflects the liver’s clearing work. A high ALT by itself does not mean liver failure.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Part of routine screening of liver health; helps diagnose or monitor liver problems and may help diagnose other conditions. It may be ordered alone but is often part of a liver function panel.

Ordered at routine checkups, to monitor treatment of a liver problem, with symptoms of liver damage (such as jaundice, nausea, abdominal swelling or pain, dark urine), or without symptoms when liver disease risk is higher (family history, alcohol use disorder, obesity, diabetes, medicines that can harm the liver, hepatitis or exposure to it).

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: AST (aspartate aminotransferase) is an enzyme found mainly in the liver, but also in the heart, muscles and other tissues. Its blood level is usually low; when the liver or other AST-containing cells are damaged, AST is released into the blood.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
bullets: High: High AST may be due to liver disease or other liver problems. Other possible causes: hepatitis, cirrhosis, mononucleosis, heart procedures or problems, pancreatitis, hemochromatosis (too much iron), deep burns, seizures, use of drugs toxic to the liver (especially alcohol) and surgery.
High: ALT is often ordered together with AST. High AST and/or ALT may mean some type of liver damage.
High: AST rising with ALT out of proportion to alkaline phosphatase indicates a cytolytic (hepatocellular) pattern; if ALP predominates, a cholestatic pattern.
Low: Low AST levels in the blood are usually considered normal.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines taken; stop any only if the provider says so. AST is usually ordered with other blood tests, which often require fasting for up to 12 hours.
Interferences: A result outside the normal range does not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Pregnancy, exercise, certain medicines, age and sex can affect the result.

Limitations: When liver test results are abnormal, the provider compares all the measured substances to look for patterns that suggest different types of liver conditions. Liver function tests alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
bullets: The De Ritis ratio is AST/ALT. Classically it is usually above 2 in alcoholic liver disease and below 1 in chronic viral hepatitis and chronic cholestasis; in non-alcoholic liver disease a ratio above 1 may suggest cirrhosis. With cirrhosis the ratio separates alcoholic from non-alcoholic causes less well. AST is also found in heart and muscle, so the ratio is meaningful only for liver conditions.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Used to screen for or help diagnose liver and bone diseases and to help diagnose or monitor other conditions. Often done with a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) or liver function tests, or when there are symptoms of liver damage or a bone disorder (bone pain, joint inflammation, unusually shaped or enlarged bones, broken bones).
Physiology: ALP is an enzyme present in all body tissues, with higher amounts in the liver, bile ducts and bones. Each part of the body makes a different type of ALP.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
bullets: High: High ALP from the liver may be a sign of bile duct blockage, cirrhosis, hepatitis or mononucleosis (which can sometimes cause swelling in the liver).

High: If ALP is high and liver tests are normal, a bone disorder such as Paget's disease of bone is possible. Moderately high ALP may occur with many conditions, including Hodgkin lymphoma, heart failure and certain infections; a high ALP may also occur without a condition that needs treatment.
High: Cholestatic pattern: alkaline phosphatase is raised out of proportion to ALT and AST. A raised GGT supports a liver source. If bilirubin rises too, bile-duct obstruction is considered.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
bullets: Low: Low ALP is less common. Possible causes: zinc deficiency, protein deficiency, malnutrition, pernicious anemia, thyroid disease, Wilson disease and hypophosphatasia (a rare genetic disease affecting bones and teeth).

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines taken; some may need to be paused, but only on the provider's advice. Because ALP is usually ordered with other blood tests, fasting for several hours is often required.

Interferences: Pregnancy can raise ALP, and children and teens may have high ALP because their bones are growing. Birth control pills and some medicines may lower ALP while others raise it, and a fatty meal before the test may cause a small increase.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
bullets: Limitations: The ALP test alone cannot tell which tissue the ALP comes from, so other tests are usually needed. An ALP isoenzyme test can show its source (not available everywhere); if liver function tests are also high, the ALP is likely of liver origin.

Abnormal liver test results don't always mean a liver problem: high ALP, for example, can be a sign of bone disease as well as liver disease. The provider also considers symptoms, medical history, liver disease risk and medicines taken.

slides.title: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Used to help diagnose liver disease, to tell liver disease from a bone disorder, to check for bile duct blockage, and to screen for or monitor alcohol use disorder. Drinking alcohol raises GGT, and most people with alcohol use disorder have high GGT.
Usually done with or after other liver tests, most often ALP. Both GGT and ALP may rise in diseases of the liver and bile ducts, but only ALP rises in bone disease.

slides.title: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: GGT is an enzyme found throughout the body but mainly in the liver. If the liver or bile ducts are damaged, GGT may leak into the bloodstream.

slides.title: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
bullets: High: High GGT may be a sign of liver damage. Possible causes include hepatitis, cirrhosis, alcohol use disorder, pancreatitis, diabetes, heart failure and medicine side effects. The result cannot show which condition is responsible, but usually the higher the GGT, the more liver damage.
High: Compared with ALP: high ALP with high GGT points to a liver disorder rather than a bone disorder, while high ALP with low or normal GGT makes a bone disorder more likely.
Low: A low or normal GGT means liver disease is unlikely.

slides.title: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Ask the provider about specific instructions; fasting for a set time before the test may be requested.
Interferences: Results may be affected by certain medicines or supplements, drinking alcohol and smoking cigarettes. GGT levels go down after meals.

Limitations: GGT cannot identify the specific cause of liver disease; it only indicates that the liver is being damaged. The provider interprets it with symptoms, medical history and other blood tests.

slides.title: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
bullets: Among liver laboratory patterns GGT belongs to the cholestatic group: rising with ALP supports a hepatobiliary cause, while a high ALP with normal GGT supports bone. GGT also rises with alcohol and some medicines, so alone it does not prove cholestasis.

slides.title: Amylase
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Blood or urine (clean-catch sample or 24-hour collection); peritoneal fluid in certain cases

What it is used for: Blood or urine amylase is mainly used to diagnose pancreatic problems, including pancreatitis, and to monitor chronic pancreatitis. It may also help diagnose or monitor treatment of salivary gland disorders and certain digestive conditions.
Changes in amylase appear in blood before urine, so a urine amylase test may be done with or after a blood test.

slides.title: Amylase
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Amylase is an enzyme that helps digest carbohydrates; most of it is made by the pancreas and the salivary glands. A small amount in blood and urine is normal, but too much may be a sign of a disorder of the pancreas, the salivary glands or another condition.

slides.title: Amylase
bullets: High: High amylase in blood or urine may be a sign of acute pancreatitis, a blocked pancreatic duct, or a cancerous or benign pancreatic tumor. High amylase in peritoneal fluid may be a sign of acute pancreatitis, a blocked intestine or lack of blood flow to the intestines.

Low: Low amylase in blood or urine is uncommon; possible causes include chronic pancreatitis with permanent damage to the amylase-producing cells, kidney disease, cystic fibrosis, liver disease and pre-eclampsia.

slides.title: Amylase
bullets: Pre-analytics: Alcohol should be avoided for 24 hours before a blood or urine amylase test, and fasting for two hours may be requested before a blood test.

Urine is usually collected by the clean-catch method; bleeding hemorrhoids or a menstrual period should be reported before the test. A 24-hour collection may be requested because urine amylase varies through the day, and it gives more accurate information.
Interferences: Prescription and over-the-counter medicines may affect the results, so they should be reported to the provider; medicines should not be stopped unless the provider says so.

slides.title: Amylase
bullets: Limitations: When pancreatitis is suspected, lipase may be ordered together with amylase. Lipase tests are considered more accurate for diagnosing pancreatitis, especially when it is caused by alcohol use disorder.

slides.title: Lipase
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Blood (venous sample)

What it is used for: Used to help diagnose pancreatic diseases, especially acute pancreatitis, and to check whether their treatment is working. It may also help diagnose and monitor chronic diseases that affect the pancreas (cystic fibrosis, Crohn's disease, celiac disease) and help diagnose intestinal injury or blockage, peritonitis and pancreatic cysts.

Physiology: Lipase is a digestive enzyme that helps the body digest fats. Most of it is made in the pancreas, with some from the salivary glands and stomach; a small amount in blood is normal, but damaged pancreatic cells release larger amounts.

slides.title: Lipase
bullets: High: A very high lipase level is usually a sign of acute pancreatitis. Other possible causes of higher-than-normal levels include pancreatic diseases (such as a blocked duct or pancreatic cancer), chronic kidney disease, peptic ulcer, gallbladder disease, intestinal problems such as a blocked intestine, diabetes, salivary gland disorders and alcohol use disorder.
Low: Low lipase may be a sign of permanent damage to the pancreatic cells that make lipase, which may happen in chronic diseases such as cystic fibrosis and chronic pancreatitis.

slides.title: Lipase
bullets: Pre-analytics: Fasting for 8 to 12 hours may be required before the blood test. Certain medicines and supplements can affect the result; the provider says whether any should be stopped, and they should not be stopped otherwise.

Interferences: An abnormal lipase result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Many medicines, including codeine, diuretics, certain cholesterol medicines and birth control pills, can affect lipase levels.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Blood; in certain cases cerebrospinal, peritoneal or pleural fluid

What it is used for: LDH is mainly used to check for tissue damage. It may help diagnose or monitor diseases of the blood (including anemia), liver, lungs, kidneys, heart (including heart attack), pancreas, brain and spinal cord, and help monitor conditions that may worsen over time, such as muscular dystrophy and HIV.

It may also help diagnose certain severe infections, show how serious some cancers are (multiple myeloma, lymphoma, leukemia, testicular cancer, melanoma) and check whether treatment for certain cancers is working.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: LDH (lactate, or lactic acid, dehydrogenase) is an enzyme that helps cells make energy and is found in almost all tissues, with the largest amounts in muscles, liver, kidneys and red blood cells. When disease or injury damages these tissues, the cells release LDH into the blood or other body fluids.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
bullets: High: In general, higher-than-normal LDH usually means some type of tissue damage, usually from disease, infection or injury; more tests may be needed to diagnose the condition.

Low: Lower-than-normal LDH is uncommon and usually not considered a health problem. Taking large amounts of vitamin C or vitamin E, or the rare genetic disorder lactate dehydrogenase deficiency, may cause low levels.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for an LDH blood test. For other fluids (cerebrospinal fluid by lumbar puncture, chest fluid by thoracentesis, abdominal fluid by paracentesis) the provider explains how to prepare.

Interferences: A high LDH does not always mean a condition that needs treatment: intense exercise and certain medicines, including aspirin, can raise it. LDH can also be high if many red blood cells broke open while the sample was collected and tested (hemolysis).

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
bullets: Limitations: An LDH test alone cannot show what is damaging tissues or where the damage is, so it is usually done with other tests. The meaning of a result depends on why the test was done, the symptoms and other test results.
If LDH is high, an LDH isoenzyme test, which measures five forms of LDH, may be ordered to help find the type and location of the damaged tissue and how serious the damage is.

slides.title: Creatine kinase (CK)
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Blood (venous sample)

What it is used for: CK is most often used to help diagnose and monitor muscle injuries (from accidents, serious burns or extreme exercise) and muscle diseases such as muscular dystrophy, rhabdomyolysis and myositis.

In certain cases CK may help diagnose a heart attack, but troponin testing is used more often because it is better at finding heart muscle damage. After a stroke, CK may be measured to find out how severe it was and help predict the chance of another stroke.

slides.title: Creatine kinase (CK)
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Testing may be needed with symptoms of a muscle disorder (muscle pain or cramps, weakness, balance problems, numbness or tingling, dark urine, swollen legs or feet), after injuries that crushed or tore muscles or serious burns, when taking medicines that may damage muscle such as statins, or after a stroke or traumatic brain injury.

Physiology: Creatine kinase (CK, also called creatine phosphokinase, CPK) is an enzyme that helps make energy. Most of it is in skeletal muscle, with some in heart muscle and small amounts in the brain; normal muscle wear releases a little CK into the blood, while damage to muscle, heart or brain releases larger amounts.

slides.title: Creatine kinase (CK)
bullets: High: A higher-than-normal CK usually means some type of muscle damage. CK may not peak until up to two days after certain injuries, so repeat tests may be done; levels that stay high or keep rising may mean ongoing muscle damage.

High: A CK isoenzyme test helps show where CK comes from: high CK-MM most likely reflects skeletal muscle damage (disease, injury, medicines or recent intense exercise), and high CK-MB most likely heart muscle damage (heart attack, myocarditis), although a blood clot in the lung, heart surgery, congestive heart failure, hypothyroidism and kidney failure can also raise it. High CK-BB may mean a stroke or brain injury, or a condition affecting smooth muscle.

slides.title: Creatine kinase (CK)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed, but to help make results accurate the provider may ask the patient to avoid intense exercise and alcohol for a few days before the test.

Limitations: Normal CK levels for a person depend on age, sex and race, muscle mass and physical activity. A CK result cannot show where the damage is or what is causing it, so symptoms and medical history are considered.

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: 2 of 3: typical pain; lipase or amylase ≥3×ULN; imaging ×ULN

slides.title: A patient's ALT is markedly high. What does the ALT level itself tell you about how much of the liver is damaged?
options: The higher the ALT, the larger the share of the liver that has been damaged
Nothing reliable — the ALT level is not related to the extent of damage
A high ALT confirms that cirrhosis is the cause of the damage
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the ALT level does not reflect the extent of damage; it is interpreted together with the other liver tests.

Basis: MedlinePlus: the amount of ALT in the blood isn't related to how much the liver may be damaged; ALT is compared with the other liver tests.

slides.title: Why is ALT considered a more liver-specific marker of damage than AST?
options: ALT is found mostly in the liver, while AST is also found in the heart, muscles and other tissues
ALT is not affected by medicines, exercise or age, so any change in it reflects the liver alone
ALT is released only when liver cancer is present, so a high ALT points to a tumor rather than other damage
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: AST can also rise when tissues outside the liver are damaged, whereas ALT comes mainly from the liver.

Basis: MedlinePlus: ALT is mostly found in the liver and checks more specifically for liver damage; AST is also found in the heart, muscles and other tissues.

slides.title: A patient with no known liver disease has a high AST. Why might the AST come from outside the liver?
options: AST is made only by red blood cells, so any AST in the blood comes from them
AST is also found in the heart, muscles and other tissues and is released when they are damaged
AST rises only when the patient has eaten before the blood draw instead of fasting as instructed
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source also lists non-liver causes of high AST, such as heart problems, deep burns, seizures and surgery.

Basis: MedlinePlus: AST is found mainly in the liver but also in the heart, muscles and other tissues; damaged AST-containing cells release it into the blood.

slides.title: How is a low AST level in the blood usually interpreted?
options: It is usually considered normal
As a sign of liver failure
As proof that the sample was collected incorrectly
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source states that low AST levels in the blood are usually considered normal.

Basis: MedlinePlus: low levels of AST in the blood are usually considered normal.

slides.title: ALP is high, but the other liver tests are normal. Which explanation does the source suggest?
options: A bile duct blockage is confirmed, even though the other liver tests are normal
The only explanation is an error in the laboratory measurement
A bone disorder, such as Paget's disease of bone, may be the cause
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: with high ALP and normal liver tests the problem may be a bone disorder; an ALP isoenzyme test can show the source.

Basis: MedlinePlus: if ALP is high and liver tests are normal, the problem may be a bone disorder such as Paget's disease of bone.

slides.title: A 14-year-old has a high ALP. Which factor from the source should be considered before assuming disease?
options: Children and teens may have high ALP because their bones are growing
Teens always have very low ALP, so this means liver failure
Age does not affect ALP, so a high value must mean bone or liver disease
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source names bone growth as a reason for high ALP in children and teens.

Basis: MedlinePlus: children and teens may have high ALP because their bones are growing.

slides.title: Enzymes, structure, classification?
bullets: 1. Enzymes are biological catalysts (mostly proteins) that lower activation energy; active site, substrate specificity; most require a cofactor/coenzyme (often vitamin derivatives).

2. Structure: simple and complex (apoenzyme + cofactor = holoenzyme); oligomeric enzymes, isoenzymes (forms catalyzing the same reaction but differing in structure and tissue distribution – for example LDH1–5, CK-MM/MB/BB).
3. International classification (IUBMB, EC numbers) – 7 classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases, translocases.

slides.title: Enzymes, structure, classification?
bullets: 4. Units of activity: the international unit (U – 1 µmol substrate/min) and the katal; in the clinic U/L, the conditions of determination (temperature 37 °C, pH, substrate) affect the result – IFCC reference procedures.
5. Clinical significance: enzymes are markers of disease (ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, amylase, lipase, CK) and laboratory reagents (methods for glucose, cholesterol, urea).

slides.title: Kinetics of enzymatic processes. Regulation of enzyme activity. Enzymopathies?
bullets: 1. Enzyme kinetics: the reaction rate depends on substrate concentration (Michaelis–Menten); Vmax is the rate when all active sites are saturated, Km is the substrate concentration at half-maximal rate (inversely related to affinity).

2. Factors affecting the rate: temperature, pH, enzyme and substrate concentrations, cofactors, inhibitors; in the laboratory activity is measured with saturating substrate under standard conditions (37 °C).

slides.title: Kinetics of enzymatic processes. Regulation of enzyme activity. Enzymopathies?
bullets: 3. Inhibition: competitive (Km rises, Vmax unchanged – overcome by increasing substrate), noncompetitive (allosteric site; Vmax decreases, Km unchanged), uncompetitive (both decrease); irreversible inhibitors (for example organophosphates – cholinesterase).

4. Regulation of activity: allosteric regulation, covalent modification (phosphorylation), activation of proenzymes (zymogens) (trypsinogen, coagulation factors), induction/repression of synthesis, compartmentalization.

slides.title: Kinetics of enzymatic processes. Regulation of enzyme activity. Enzymopathies?
bullets: 5. Enzymopathies: inherited enzyme defects – phenylketonuria, galactosemia, glycogen storage diseases, G6PD deficiency, pseudocholinesterase deficiency; acquired – changes in enzyme activity in diseases.

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of alkaline and acid phosphatase and methods of determination?
bullets: 1. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) – isoenzymes: non-tissue-specific (liver, bone, kidney) and specific (intestinal, placental, germ cell); the main part in the blood is liver and bone.
2. Determination: kinetic method with a chromogenic phosphate substrate (IFCC reference procedure, 37 °C); isoenzymes can be separated by electrophoresis or immunoassay (bone ALP).

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of alkaline and acid phosphatase and methods of determination?
bullets: 3. Increase: cholestasis (together with GGT), bone diseases (Paget, metastases, osteomalacia, rickets, hyperparathyroidism), growth period, pregnancy (placenta), after a fatty meal the intestinal isoenzyme (in blood groups O and B) – fasting collection is recommended.
4. Acid phosphatase was historically a marker of prostate cancer; replaced by PSA as more accurate; tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase is a marker of osteoclast activity.
5. Interpretation: when ALP is raised, determine the source by GGT (liver) or bone markers.
